What the official sources say

  • Louisiana Tax Commission hears real and personal property appeals from board of review actions; hearings begin within ten days of receiving the certified assessment lists. (La. R.S. 47:1989; source)
  • Taxpayer dissatisfied with a final Tax Commission decision may sue within thirty days in the district court for the parish where the Commission is domiciled or where the property is located. (La. R.S. 47:1998; source)
  • A taxpayer who sues must pay taxes under protest (or timely move to set bond/security); undisputed taxes are paid without protest. (La. R.S. 47:1998; source)
  • Board of review hears owners' complaints on assessments; its determinations are final unless appealed to the Tax Commission under Commission rules. (La. R.S. 47:1992 (board of review); source)
  • Board of review must convene hearings on or before September 15 and certify the list to the Tax Commission on or before October 20 each year; assessors certify rolls to the board on or before October 1. (La. R.S. 47:1992 (board of review); source)
  • Since Acts 2024 No. 774 and Acts 2025 No. 411 (eff. Jan. 1, 2026), Louisiana auctions tax liens rather than the property at first stage; winner gets a recorded tax lien certificate. (La. R.S. 47:2153; source)
  • Auction participants may be required to post a deposit up to $1,000. (La. R.S. 47:2153(C)(5); source)

How does Louisiana property tax work?

Louisiana property tax is built locally: a parish assessor sets the value, local voters approve the millage rates, and the parish sheriff usually collects the bill. The state constitution fixes the assessment percentages, and the Louisiana Tax Commission hears the appeals that come up from local boards.

Louisiana has parishes where most states have counties. Wikipedia's Louisiana article notes it is one of only two states without counties, and it reports a 2020 census population of 4,657,757. For a seller that means the office you deal with is the parish assessor and the parish sheriff, whether the house is in New Orleans, Baton Rouge or a small town.

The East Baton Rouge Parish Sheriff's office puts the division of labor plainly: the sheriff does not decide how much you owe. The assessed value comes from the assessor, and the millage comes from votes by residents of the parish.

What percentage of value is taxed in Louisiana?

Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value, while other property is assessed at 15%. Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution sets these levels, and it also sets 25% for public service property other than land.

Property typeAssessment level
Land10%
Residential improvements10%
Other property15%
Public service property (not land)25%

Property must be reappraised at intervals of no more than four years. When a reappraisal pushes the assessed value of a homestead-exempt house up by more than 50% over the year before, the added tax is phased in over four years. That phase-in ends when the property changes hands, so a buyer may face the full figure that a long-time owner never paid. The constitution also holds the assessment level for qualifying owners, including those 65 or older, subject to an income limit.

The legislature's text of section 18 has the full wording.

How is a Louisiana tax bill calculated, with an example?

Take the fair market value, subtract any homestead exemption, apply the 10% level, then multiply by the total millage. The St. James Parish Assessor posts worked examples that show every step.

StepExample 1Example 2
Fair market value$100,000$150,000
Less homestead exemption$75,000$75,000
Taxable value$25,000$75,000
Assessed value at 10%$2,500$7,500
Bill at 10.703 percent millage$267.58$802.73

That parish's page uses a 10.703 percent rate for illustration, and rates differ from parish to parish and from one tax district to the next. The same page points out how sharply the bill moves: because the $75,000 exemption stays fixed, each extra $25,000 of value adds $267.58 in its example. Look at the assessor's page to see the layout.

The East Baton Rouge sheriff adds a caution. The homestead exemption covers parish taxes only, so city taxes and fire or crime fees are still owed on the full amount.

What does the homestead exemption cover?

The homestead exemption removes parish property tax on the first $75,000 of a home's market value, which is $7,500 of assessed value. Owners must apply with the parish assessor, and the home must be their primary residence.

  • It applies to one home per owner.
  • The East Baton Rouge Parish Assessor says the owner must own and occupy the residence by December 31 of the tax year.
  • It does not reduce city taxes or fire and crime district fees in East Baton Rouge Parish.
  • A tax sale can cost the owner the exemption.

For sellers this matters in an odd way. The exemption attaches to an owner who lives in the home, so a buyer who will not occupy it would not qualify. That means your current bill may understate what the next owner pays. A seller who is asked about taxes should say so plainly.

When are Louisiana property taxes due, and what happens after?

Taxes for the year are due by December 31, and the roll normally reaches the collector by November 15. The sheriff mails bills in the last week of November, and the St. James assessor's page gives the same schedule.

  • After December 31 the taxes are delinquent, and interest runs at 1% per month.
  • The East Baton Rouge sheriff adds a collection fee if taxes are unpaid after January 31, followed by certified notice and advertising costs.
  • La. R.S. 47:2153 has the tax collector send certified mail by the first Monday of February, with 20 days to pay before the lien is auctioned.
  • A deposit of up to $1,000 may be required from bidders.

Louisiana's newer process auctions a tax lien before it auctions the house. The winning bidder gets a recorded tax lien certificate. The owner keeps ownership and possession until a court judgment is executed, and during that time the lienholder may not evict the owner or collect rent. To get the lien released, the owner pays the auction price, interest of up to 1% a month, a 5% penalty and costs, and this can be done any time before an enforcement action is filed.

The EBR sheriff's FAQ describes the older tax sale process, under which a property sold could be redeemed within three years from recordation with a 5% penalty plus 1% interest a month. Parishes may differ on timing, so check which process your parish runs.

How do you appeal a Louisiana property assessment?

You start with the parish assessor and the board of review, and only then go to the Louisiana Tax Commission and district court. Each step has a short window, so owners who wait lose the chance.

StepWhat the statute says
Request a written notice of assessmentAsk no earlier than June 1; the assessor must receive it by June 15 (R.S. 47:1992)
Inspection of the roll15 days between August 15 and September 15 in most parishes; July 15 to August 15 in Orleans
Board of review complaintGive the board at least seven days' notice; the board may raise or lower the value
Appeal to the Tax CommissionHearings begin within ten days of receiving the certified lists (R.S. 47:1989)
District courtFile within thirty days of the commission's decision

The board of review must convene hearings on or before September 15 and certify its list to the Tax Commission by October 20, and the assessor certifies the rolls to the board on or before October 1. The Tax Commission may affirm, remand, reverse or modify an assessment. A taxpayer who sues pays the disputed amount under protest, and under R.S. 47:1998 the undisputed part is paid without protest.

The statutes are on Justia: R.S. 47:1992 and R.S. 47:1989.

What happens to property taxes when you sell a house in Louisiana?

Taxes follow the property, and the sheriff does not split them between buyer and seller. The East Baton Rouge sheriff states that tax, interest, penalties and fees stay in effect until paid regardless of who owns the property, and that any private agreement between the two sides does not bind the collector.

A sale after January 1 can leave the bill in the previous owner's name on the roll, because the assessor sets values as of January 1. The buyer must still check whether taxes are owed. Louisiana also lets an assessor add omitted property for up to three back years under R.S. 47:1966, so a house missing from the roll can generate a catch-up bill.

  • Ask the sheriff's tax office for the account balance before listing or signing.
  • Settle the current year's bill at closing and put the split in writing.
  • Under R.S. 9:2721, the deed names the person responsible for property taxes and the address for notices, so that detail must be right.
  • Confirm the homestead exemption status with the assessor.

If back taxes are already piling up, we can look at the house as it stands and explain how the payoff would work at closing.

More questions about Louisiana Property Tax Guide

What is the Louisiana homestead exemption?

It removes parish property tax on the first $75,000 of a primary residence's value, which is $7,500 of assessed value. You apply through the parish assessor. City taxes and fire or crime fees in East Baton Rouge are not covered.

When are Louisiana property taxes due?

Taxes are due by December 31 of the tax year. Bills are mailed in late November, and interest at 1% a month starts after December 31. A collection fee and advertising costs can follow after January 31.

What percent of value is a Louisiana home assessed at?

Land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value under Article VII, section 18 of the Louisiana Constitution. Other property is assessed at 15%. Reappraisal must happen at least every four years.

Can I sell my Louisiana house with back taxes owed?

Yes, but the taxes are paid out of the proceeds or by the buyer at closing, since they stay attached to the property. A recorded tax lien must be cleared before clean title passes. The sheriff will give you a payoff figure.

How do I dispute my Louisiana assessment?

Ask the assessor for the notice, then bring a complaint to the parish board of review during its hearing window. A board decision can be appealed to the Louisiana Tax Commission, and then to district court within thirty days of the commission's decision.

Who collects property tax in Louisiana?

The parish sheriff, acting as tax collector, sends and collects the bills. The parish assessor sets the value, and local voters approve the millage rates.

title: Louisiana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

Louisiana Homestead Exemption: Eligibility, Filing and Selling the Home

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Since land and residential improvements are assessed at 10% of fair market value, the $7,500 assessed exemption corresponds to $75,000 of market value (arithmetic from the two cited provisions). (La. Const. art. VII, secs. 18(A), 20(A)(1); source)

What does the Louisiana homestead exemption actually exempt?

The homestead exemption takes the first $7,500 of assessed value off the property tax base of an owner-occupied home. That figure comes from Article VII, section 20 of the Louisiana Constitution, which covers state, parish and special ad valorem taxes on a bona fide homestead.

The constitution lets the homestead be a residence plus a field, pasture or garden on other tracts, as long as the total does not run past 160 acres. A primary residence that is a mobile home qualifies even when the owner does not own the land, although the land itself gets no exemption in that case.

Because residential improvements and land are assessed at 10 percent of fair market value under Article VII, section 18, a $7,500 cut in assessed value lines up with roughly $75,000 of market value. The tax savings depend on the millage in your parish, so two homeowners with identical houses can see different dollar results.

Who qualifies, and who does not?

Section 20 limits the exemption to natural persons and to trusts that natural persons created for natural-person beneficiaries. A company cannot claim it, and neither can an owner who does not live in the house.

  • Surviving or former spouses who occupy the homestead can keep the exemption if they hold title as owner, as usufructuary or through a testamentary trust.
  • Property held in indivision gets only the occupying owner's pro rata share of the exemption.
  • Property bought on a bond for deed gets no exemption under the current text, with a carve-out for exemptions granted before June 20, 2003.
  • No person may receive more than one homestead exemption in the state.

The one-per-person rule matters if you own two houses. Selling the old one after you move does not create a second exemption, and the new home needs its own claim.

Does the exemption cover city and town taxes?

Generally no. The constitution excludes municipal taxes from the exemption, with an exception for Orleans Parish (state, general city, school, levee and levee district taxes) and for municipal taxes levied for school purposes.

That is why a homeowner inside a municipality may find the exemption saves less than the $7,500 figure suggests. Check the tax bill line by line, or ask the parish assessor which levies the exemption reaches.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens to the exemption after a storm?

A homeowner whose house was damaged or destroyed in a governor-declared disaster can keep the exemption while rebuilding. Under section 20(A)(10), an owner who cannot move back in by December 31 files an annual affidavit of intent to return, good for up to five years.

After that, the owner can keep the exemption for up to two more years if an insurance claim or a formal appeal is still pending, with official documentation. The assessor may then grant up to three more one-year extensions case by case.

This matters for sellers of storm-damaged houses. If you plan to sell rather than rebuild, the exemption stops mattering once title passes, and the new owner starts fresh.

How do the age 65 freeze and the veteran exemptions fit in?

These are separate programs from the homestead exemption, and each one is filed with the parish assessor. The age-based assessment freeze sits in section 18(G) of Article VII, and the disabled veteran exemptions sit in section 21(K).

ProgramWhat the constitution text says
Special assessment level (age 65 or older, certain disabled veterans and others)Assessment is held at the first qualifying year's total. Signed application to the assessor. Income cap listed as $100,000 until January 1, 2027, then $150,000. Ends December 31 of the year before the property is sold.
Veteran, 50% to under 70% service-connected disabilityNext $2,500 of assessed value exempt after the $7,500 homestead amount
Veteran, 70% to under 100%Next $4,500 of assessed value exempt
Veteran at 100% unemployability or total disabilityRemaining assessed value of the homestead exempt

Section 21 also describes an extra age-based exemption starting January 1, 2028, which needs voter approval in the parish or municipality. Do not count on it until your own parish confirms it was adopted.

Is a protection from creditors the same thing as a tax exemption?

No. Louisiana has a second homestead concept in R.S. 20:1 that shields the home from seizure and sale by creditors, and it works differently from the tax break.

  • It protects the first $35,000 in value of the homestead, and the full value when debts come from a catastrophic or terminal illness or injury that meets the statute's definition.
  • The protected land is up to 5 acres when the residence is in a municipality and up to 200 acres when it is not.
  • It covers the owner-occupant and the surviving spouse or minor children of a deceased owner.
  • It does not protect against debts for the purchase price, taxes or assessments, rent carrying a privilege, mortgage advances, or work done to build or improve the home.

A waiver of this protection has to be in writing, be signed (by the spouse too, if the owner is married and not legally separated), and be recorded in the mortgage records of the parish.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

How do you claim the homestead exemption?

You file with the assessor in the parish where the house stands, and the local assessor's office is the authority on forms and timing. Louisiana has 64 parishes and each has one elected assessor, according to the Legislative Auditor's guide to assessors.

The Loyola law school pro bono desk manual notes that assessors generally grant retroactive exemptions for the last three years when an owner discovers a missed claim. It also says an assessor may decline if a will is involved, so heirs who inherit a house should bring the succession paperwork.

When you buy or inherit a house, remember R.S. 9:2721. A conveyance of immovable property filed with the parish recorder must name the person responsible for property taxes and give a mailing address for tax notices, and that person must give the information to the assessor.

What does a sale do to the exemption and the tax bill?

A sale ends the seller's claim, and the buyer applies for a new one if the buyer will live in the house. The age freeze is even more direct: the constitution says it generally expires December 31 of the year before the property is sold, and the house is then valued at fair market value.

Section 18(F) adds another wrinkle. When a reappraisal pushes the assessed value of homestead-exempt property up by more than 50 percent, the increase is phased in over four years, but that phase-in ends early when ownership transfers. A buyer can therefore face a full reassessment sooner than the seller did.

Unpaid taxes follow the land. The Loyola desk manual explains that ad valorem taxes are a charge on the immovable, tax sales are run under Article VII, section 25 and R.S. 47:2121 and following, and a debtor who redeems pays the taxes, costs, a 5 percent penalty and simple interest of 1 percent per month. The redemption period is three years from recording of the tax sale certificate, or 18 months for blighted property.

What should a Louisiana seller check before listing or taking a cash offer?

  • Confirm on your latest tax notice that the homestead exemption is applied. If it is missing, ask the assessor about back claims.
  • List any freeze, veteran or disability exemption you hold, because they end or change when title moves.
  • Check for unpaid taxes or a prior tax sale certificate recorded against the property.
  • Gather the succession judgment or affidavit if you inherited the house, since the assessor and any buyer will want to see how title reached you.
  • Ask the clerk of court or your closing notary which recording fees apply, since fees vary with the number of pages.

A cash buyer works through the same recording and tax steps as any other buyer, so these items should be tidy either way. If a house has a tax problem or a messy succession, say so early, because it affects how fast a sale can close.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

More questions about Louisiana Homestead Exemption

How much is the Louisiana homestead exemption?

It is $7,500 of assessed value on an owner-occupied home. Since homes are assessed at 10 percent of market value, that matches about $75,000 of market value, and the actual savings depend on your local millage.

Can I claim a homestead exemption on a rental house?

No. The exemption is for a bona fide homestead that the owner occupies, and the constitution allows only one per person in Louisiana. A landlord can claim it only on the home where they actually live.

Does the homestead exemption transfer to the buyer when I sell?

No. It belongs to the owner who occupies the home, so the buyer files a new claim with the assessor. The age 65 assessment freeze also ends when the house is sold.

Does the exemption stop a creditor from forcing a sale?

Not by itself. The tax exemption and the creditor protection in R.S. 20:1 are separate rules, and the creditor protection has its own limit of $35,000 and a list of debts it does not cover, such as the purchase price and unpaid taxes.

Do I keep the exemption if a hurricane makes my house unlivable?

Yes, in many cases. Under section 20(A)(10) you file an annual affidavit of intent to return, which can protect the exemption for up to five years, with further extensions in some situations.

title: Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Louisiana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Louisiana inheritance tax law (R.S. 47:2401-2426) was repealed by Act 822 of 2008; no inheritance tax receipts issued after January 1, 2012. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)
  • Estate transfer tax (R.S. 47:2431-2437) equals the federal state death tax credit; because that credit is repealed, no state estate transfer tax is due for deaths after December 31, 2004. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)
  • R.S. 47:2436 requires an estate transfer tax return where tax is due or the net estate is $60,000 or more. (Inheritance and Estate Transfer Taxes | Louisiana Department of Revenue; source)
Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Louisiana have an estate tax or inheritance tax?

No state death tax is due on a Louisiana estate today. The state repealed its inheritance tax, and its estate transfer tax only ever existed to capture a federal credit that no longer exists.

According to the Louisiana Department of Revenue, Act 822 of the 2008 Regular Session repealed the inheritance tax law in R.S. 47:2401 to 2426, and from January 1, 2012 no receipts are issued for inheritance tax regardless of the date of death. The estate transfer tax in R.S. 47:2431 to 2437 equals the federal credit for state death taxes. Because that credit was replaced by a deduction for deaths after December 31, 2004, the department says no state estate transfer tax is due for those deaths.

For heirs of a Louisiana house, that means the sale proceeds are not reduced by a state death tax. The money questions that remain are federal, plus the cost and time of moving title.

What does Louisiana law still ask heirs to file?

One filing rule stays on the books: an estate transfer tax return is required where tax is due or where the deceased's net estate is $60,000 or more. R.S. 47:2436 says the heirs or legatees file it, and that it is mailed to the collector of revenue and to the person designated as tax collector under R.S. 47:2417.

The statute sets the timing at nine months after death, or before a United States estate tax return is filed, whichever comes first. It also requires the return to list the full name of the deceased, residence at death, estate value, whether a federal return was filed, safety deposit box contents omitted from the estate and any omitted assets, with an explanation.

The Revenue Department's page was last updated on February 20, 2025. Whether a return is still expected on an estate with no tax due is a question for the succession attorney or a CPA, since the page and statute both keep the $60,000 trigger in place.

How much of an estate does the federal government tax in 2026?

Only large estates owe federal estate tax: the basic exclusion amount for people who die in 2026 is $15,000,000. The IRS states that the Working Families Tax Cuts law, signed July 4, 2025, raised the basic exclusion amount to that level.

The same IRS page lists the annual gift exclusion for 2026 as $19,000 per donee. Estates under the exclusion amount owe no federal estate tax, and the filing threshold for year-of-death 2026 is also $15,000,000.

ItemAmount or ruleSource
Louisiana inheritance taxRepealed, no receipts since Jan. 1, 2012Louisiana Department of Revenue
Louisiana estate transfer taxNone due for deaths after Dec. 31, 2004Louisiana Department of Revenue
Estate transfer tax returnRequired if net estate is $60,000 or more (R.S. 47:2436)Louisiana Legislature
Federal basic exclusion, 2026 death$15,000,000IRS
Federal annual gift exclusion, 2026$19,000 per doneeIRS

Will an heir who sells an inherited Louisiana house owe income tax?

An heir's gain is usually figured from the home's value on the date of death, not from what the deceased paid. The IRS explains that the basis of inherited property is generally the fair market value on the decedent's date of death, whether or not the executor files a federal estate tax return.

That is why a house inherited and sold soon afterward often produces little or no taxable gain. The gain, if any, is the sale price less that stepped basis and allowed selling costs. Two cases deserve a closer look:

  • Community property: IRS Publication 551 says that when either spouse dies, the total value of community property, even the part belonging to the survivor, generally becomes the basis of the entire property.
  • Special valuation: for some farm or business property and for property whose value is set under estate tax rules, the basis can follow that valuation instead.

Keep the date-of-death appraisal. Pub. 551 notes that if no Schedule A reports the estate tax value, the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes can establish basis, so a written valuation helps in any case.

How does an heir get legal title to sell a Louisiana house?

A house cannot be sold by heirs just because the owner died; title has to be moved to them through a succession. Louisiana does this through a court proceeding that ends in a judgment of possession, or through a sworn affidavit when the estate qualifies as a small succession.

Code of Civil Procedure art. 3062 says a judgment of possession in a succession is prima facie evidence of the relationship of the parties recognized in it, as heir, legatee, surviving spouse in community or usufructuary, and of their right to possess the estate. A title company will look for that judgment or the equivalent paperwork before it insures a sale.

Louisiana's approach to a surviving spouse also differs from most states. Civil Code art. 890 gives the surviving spouse a usufruct over the decedent's share of the community property, to the extent the decedent has not disposed of it by will, when descendants survive. The usufruct ends when the surviving spouse dies or remarries. A usufruct is an interest in the house, so it must be addressed in the paperwork before a sale.

When can a Louisiana family skip court with a small succession affidavit?

Some estates do not need to be opened judicially. Code of Civil Procedure art. 3431 lists three situations:

  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died intestate.
  • A person domiciled in Louisiana who died testate leaving no immovable property in Louisiana, if the surviving spouse and all persons who would inherit, with or without the testament, agree to waive probate.
  • A person domiciled outside Louisiana who died intestate or whose testament was probated by court order of another state.

Under art. 3432, at least two persons, including the surviving spouse if there is one and at least one heir, sign a sworn affidavit. With no surviving spouse, at least two heirs sign, and if there is only one heir a second person with actual knowledge signs too. The affidavit sets out the date of death and domicile, marital status, heirs and their relationships, a description of the property sufficient to identify immovable property for transfer, the value of each item and the total, and each heir's interest.

An heir who does not sign must either be unlocatable after reasonable diligence or have received thirty days' written notice by U.S. mail and not objected. Signing the affidavit also accepts the succession for an heir, so families should understand the debts of the estate first.

What happens to the property tax, mortgage and utilities while an estate is open?

Those bills keep running whether or not a succession has been opened. The estate tax rules above say nothing about carrying costs, so the heirs generally cover them or the sale proceeds do.

Practical points for a Louisiana family handling a vacant house:

  • Keep insurance active, and ask the carrier how a vacant house is treated.
  • Notify the lender and the parish assessor's office of the death if mail is going to the old address.
  • Photograph the condition of the house and keep copies of repair bills in case an executor or other heir questions the sale price.

Where heirs disagree, a cash offer does not settle the dispute, but a signed judgment or affidavit does give all of them one version of who owns what.

How does a cash sale work when the house is in an open Louisiana estate?

A cash buyer can close once title is in the hands of the people who are entitled to sell, so the first step is the same as for any buyer: prove authority. Expect to provide the judgment of possession or the filed affidavit, a copy of any will, and payoff information on liens.

Many heirs live out of state and cannot clear out a house, cut the grass or fix storm damage from a distance. Selling as-is spares them those chores. The estate and tax numbers above matter most for deciding what to do with the proceeds, so a call with an estate attorney or CPA before closing is time well spent. Our team does not give legal or tax advice; this guide only collects what the official sources say.

More questions about Louisiana Estate and Inheritance Tax

Does Louisiana charge an inheritance tax?

No. The Louisiana Department of Revenue says Act 822 of 2008 repealed the inheritance tax, and no inheritance tax receipts are issued since January 1, 2012, regardless of date of death.

Does Louisiana have a state estate tax in 2026?

No state estate transfer tax is due for deaths after December 31, 2004, according to the Department of Revenue, because the federal credit it relied on was replaced by a deduction.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for a death in 2026?

$15,000,000. The IRS states the basic exclusion amount for 2026 is $15,000,000 under the law signed July 4, 2025.

Is the sale of an inherited house in Louisiana taxable?

Only the gain above the stepped-up basis is taxable. The IRS says inherited property generally takes the fair market value on the date of death as its basis, so little gain is common when the sale follows soon after.

Do I need a court case to sell my parent's house in Louisiana?

Not always. A small succession affidavit can be used when art. 3431 allows it, such as an intestate Louisiana domiciliary. Estates with a will covering Louisiana land generally need a judicial succession.

Who gets the house when a Louisiana spouse dies?

It depends on the will and the heirs. If descendants survive, the surviving spouse has a usufruct over the decedent's share of community property under Civil Code art. 890, until death or remarriage, unless the decedent disposed of it by will.

content:
Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Lessor must give written notice to vacate allowing at least five days from delivery; for definite-term leases notice may be given up to 30 days before term ends. (La. C.C.P. art. 4701; source)
  • A lessee may waive the notice in a written lease clause. (La. C.C.P. art. 4701; source)
  • Transfer of the leased thing by the lessor does not terminate the lease; tenant may sue lessor for loss from the transfer. (La. C.C. art. 2711; source)
  • Buyer of property subject to a recorded lease takes subject to its provisions if the lease was recorded before the buyer's document. (La. R.S. 9:2721(B); source)
Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How does an eviction work in Louisiana, step by step?

A Louisiana eviction is a fast, summary court case that begins only after a written notice to vacate has gone unanswered. The steps below follow the Code of Civil Procedure, title XI, which governs the eviction of tenants and occupants.

  1. The lessor or owner delivers a written notice to vacate (art. 4701 or 4702).
  2. If the tenant or occupant does not comply, the owner has the court cite them to appear by a rule to show cause why possession should not be delivered (art. 4731). The rule states the grounds.
  3. The court makes the rule returnable no earlier than the third day after service, tries it and hears any defense (art. 4732(A)).
  4. If the owner wins, or the tenant fails to answer or appear, the court renders a judgment of eviction immediately (art. 4732(B)).
  5. If the tenant has not complied within twenty-four hours, the court issues a warrant to its sheriff, constable or marshal to deliver possession to the owner (art. 4733).

Our companion guide on the eviction notice covers step one in detail. This page picks up at the courthouse.

Which Louisiana court hears an eviction?

A justice of the peace court can hear a residential eviction, and so can the parish or district court. Code of Civil Procedure art. 4912 gives justice of the peace courts jurisdiction, concurrent with the parish or district court, over suits by landowners or lessors to evict occupants or tenants of leased residential premises, regardless of the amount of monthly or yearly rent.

The article also covers some commercial and farm leases. A justice of the peace court may hear evictions of tenants of leased commercial premises and farmland where monthly rent does not exceed $5,000, again regardless of the rent due or the rent for the rest of the lease.

Which courthouse an owner uses depends on where the house sits. For houses in a parish with city courts, parish courts or justice of the peace wards, the clerk of court can say where eviction rules are filed.

How long does each stage of a Louisiana eviction take?

The statute fixes short minimum windows, and real calendars depend on the court. The table gathers the statutory numbers.

StageStatutory timeArticle
Notice to vacateAt least 5 days from deliveryC.C.P. 4701
Hearing on the ruleNot earlier than the third day after serviceC.C.P. 4732(A)
Judgment of eviction effectiveFor not less than 90 daysC.C.P. 4732(B)
Voluntary complianceWithin 24 hours of the judgmentC.C.P. 4733
Suspensive appeal request and bondWithin 24 hours of the judgmentC.C.P. 4735

Adding the minimums, the fastest lawful path takes more than a week from notice delivery, and that assumes the owner files promptly and the court has a hearing slot. We did not find an official average length for Louisiana evictions, so we do not quote one.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What happens at the hearing?

The judge tries the rule on the day it is returnable and hears any defense the tenant raises. The owner should arrive with the lease if there is one, the written notice and proof of when it was delivered, and a record of what is owed.

A tenant who does not answer or appear loses by default: art. 4732(B) says the court shall render a judgment of eviction immediately if the owner is entitled to relief or the lessee or occupant fails to answer or appear. The resulting judgment is effective for not less than ninety days, which gives the owner a window to carry out the order rather than a single day.

Owners who are family members, heirs or buyers should bring documents that show they now hold the lessor's position. Art. 4704 defines lessor to include an assignee or transferee, so title paperwork matters.

Can a tenant appeal an eviction judgment in Louisiana?

Yes, but an appeal does not stop the eviction by itself. Under art. 4735, execution of the judgment is suspended only if the defendant answered the rule under oath pleading an affirmative defense that would entitle them to keep possession, applied for the appeal and filed the appeal bond within twenty-four hours after the judgment.

The amount of the suspensive appeal bond is set by the court, in an amount sufficient to protect the appellee against damage from the appeal. For the owner, the practical effect is that the twenty-four hour window usually decides whether the warrant for possession can issue.

What can a landlord not do while an eviction is in progress?

An owner who skips the court process risks a penalty. Art. 4731(C)(2) says that a lessor's failure to follow that article lets a residential lessee recover $500 or twice the monthly rent, whichever is greater, and the tenant may seek a restraining order or injunction. The court may award costs and attorney fees to the prevailing party.

After a federally declared disaster, the same article adds a thirty day protection for residents of the declared parishes: a household that has left the home is not treated as having abandoned it during that time. For Louisiana sellers whose rental was hit by a hurricane or flood, that matters when deciding whether the house can be treated as vacant.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Does selling a rented house in Louisiana end the lease?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 provides that the transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the lessor and lessee agreed otherwise. The buyer steps into the picture with the tenant already in the house.

Whether the buyer is bound by the lease depends on recording. Under art. 2712, a third person who acquires an immovable subject to an unrecorded lease is not bound by it, and the lessee, absent a contrary clause in the lease, has an action against the lessor for losses caused by the transfer. R.S. 9:2721 goes the other way for recorded leases: a buyer of property subject to a recorded lease that is not divested by the acquisition takes the property subject to all of its provisions. The statute says this includes any provision for paying a commission to a leasing agent.

A seller should therefore find out before listing whether the lease was ever recorded in the parish conveyance records, and what it says about rent, term and early termination.

What happens to the tenant's security deposit when a Louisiana landlord sells?

The deposit moves with the property. R.S. 9:3251(B) says that when the lessor's interest is transferred during the lease, the transferor must also transfer the deposit to the successor, and the transferor is then relieved of further liability for it. The transferee becomes responsible for returning it when the lease ends.

The general deposit rule in subsection (A) requires return to a residential tenant within one month after the lease ends. The landlord may keep what is reasonably needed to remedy a default or unreasonable wear, and if any is retained, an itemized statement with reasons is due within that month. The tenant must give a forwarding address, and the one-month rule does not apply where the tenant abandons the premises.

Sellers should write the deposit amount into the sale paperwork so it is credited correctly at closing.

Should a Louisiana owner finish the eviction before selling?

It depends on the lease, the case and the owner's patience. Finishing the eviction clears the house for showings, but it takes court time and may mean cleanup of what the tenant leaves behind.

Owners weighing the choice usually compare:

  • Cost and time of finishing a case, including repairs after the tenant leaves.
  • Whether the lease is recorded and would bind a buyer under R.S. 9:2721.
  • Whether the tenant is paying and wants to stay, which changes the picture entirely.
  • A sale as-is with the tenant in place, which transfers the lease and the deposit to the buyer under the statutes above.

Our team also looks at houses that come with tenants or a difficult rental history. The statutes above describe the rules; a Louisiana attorney can advise on a specific lease.

More questions about Louisiana Eviction Process and Selling a Rented House

How long does a Louisiana eviction take after the notice period?

The court may set the hearing no earlier than the third day after service of the rule. If the owner wins, the tenant has twenty-four hours to comply before a warrant issues. Actual timing depends on the court's calendar.

Which court handles evictions in Louisiana?

Justice of the peace courts have concurrent jurisdiction with parish or district courts over residential evictions under art. 4912, whatever the rent. The parish or district court can also hear them.

How long is a Louisiana judgment of eviction good for?

At least ninety days, under art. 4732(B). This gives the owner time to obtain a warrant and have possession delivered.

Does an appeal stop a Louisiana eviction?

Only in narrow cases. The tenant must have answered under oath pleading an affirmative defense, and must apply for the appeal and file the bond within twenty-four hours of the judgment.

Does the lease end if I sell my rented Louisiana house?

No. Civil Code art. 2711 says transfer of the leased thing does not terminate the lease unless the parties agreed otherwise. A recorded lease binds the buyer under R.S. 9:2721, while an unrecorded lease does not bind a third-party buyer under art. 2712.

What happens to my tenant's deposit if I sell the house?

You must transfer it to the buyer, and you are then relieved of further liability. The buyer must return it at the end of the lease within the time R.S. 9:3251(A) requires.

Louisiana Quitclaim Deed: Recording, Fees and When It Works

Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Quitclaim Deed sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Quitclaim Deed offer down and you owe us nothing

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • Recording fees: $100 for 1-5 pages, $200 for 6-25 pages, $300 for 26-50 pages, plus $5 per page over 50; separate fees if recorded in both mortgage and conveyance records. (La. R.S. 13:844; source)
Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does Louisiana have a quitclaim deed?

Louisiana law has no form called a quitclaim deed. The closest thing is a transfer of whatever rights the seller holds, with no guarantee that those rights exist, which Civil Code article 2502 allows.

That article says a person may transfer the rights he has in a thing without warranting them. The transferor does not owe a refund of the price if the transferee is later evicted, and the transfer cannot be rescinded for lesion. Louisiana is a civil law state, so its deed vocabulary follows the Civil Code, and the Orleans Parish clerk lists a Cash Sale, a Credit Sale and a Warranty Deed as the usual sale documents.

Expect the document you sign to carry a Civil Code title such as an act of sale, rather than the words quitclaim deed. The Orleans clerk, for example, describes a deed as an Act of Sale that may take the form of a Cash Sale, Credit Sale or Warranty Deed.

What does a transfer without warranty do and not do?

It moves the seller's rights as they stand, and the buyer takes the risk that those rights are weaker than hoped. Article 2502 adds two points that matter to anyone using this route.

  • The transfer does not raise a presumption that the buyer acted in bad faith.
  • It counts as a just title for acquisitive prescription, so a buyer who then holds the land can build toward ten years of possession.
  • If the seller later acquires ownership of the thing, that later title does not pass to the buyer.
  • The seller does not guarantee the price will be refunded if a third party wins the property.

A full sale works differently. Under article 2503, the warranty against eviction is implied in every sale, and the parties may enlarge or limit it. Even if they exclude it, the seller must still return the price if the buyer is evicted, unless the buyer clearly knew of the risk, declared the purchase to be at his own risk, or the refund duty was expressly excluded. The seller is always liable for an eviction caused by his own act, and any contrary agreement is void.

Article 2500 describes what eviction means: the buyer's loss, or danger of losing, the whole or part of the thing sold because of a third party's earlier right, including undisclosed encumbrances.

What form must a Louisiana deed take?

A transfer of immovable property must be made by authentic act or by an act under private signature. Article 1839 says so, and a transfer made orally can bind the parties only in narrow circumstances, where the property was delivered and the transferor admits the transfer under oath.

An authentic act under article 1833 is a writing executed before a notary public or other authorized officer and two witnesses. The parties, the witnesses and the notary all sign. If a party cannot sign, the notary has that party make a mark.

RequirementSource
Written transfer of immovable property, authentic act or private signatureC.C. art. 1839
Notary or other officer plus two witnesses for an authentic actC.C. art. 1833
Effect against third persons only from filing in the parishC.C. art. 1839
Person responsible for taxes and notice address named in the deedLa. R.S. 9:2721

The authentic act is the form that needs a notary, which is why closings usually run through one.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Where and how is a Louisiana deed recorded?

It is filed with the clerk of court, acting as recorder, in the parish where the property sits. Until it is filed there, the instrument does not bind third persons.

The Orleans Parish clerk shows how the system runs. The Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street takes documents by mail, in person or through eRecording vendors, and a cover sheet tells the office to record the document in the mortgage records, the conveyance records, or both. The clerk's staff cannot say which documents to file.

Every deed filed in Louisiana must also name the person responsible for taxes and give the mailing address for tax notices. That person must pass the details to the assessor, so notices go to the right place.

Parish clerks set their own hours, payment methods and add-on charges, so call the office before sending a check.

How much does recording a Louisiana deed cost?

The base fee under La. R.S. 13:844 is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, with $5 for each page above 50.

ItemFee under R.S. 13:844
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100
Recording, 6 to 25 pages$200
Recording, 26 to 50 pages$300
Each name indexed after ten$5
Mortgage certificate, first name$20, then $10 per name
Cancelling a single mortgage$50

The base fee includes indexing up to ten names and one certified copy. A document recorded in both the mortgage and conveyance records is charged separately for each. Paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches carries an extra $20 a page.

Orleans Parish adds a $5 remote access portal fee and a $30 courthouse building fund fee per recording, and the city charges a $325 documentary transaction tax on sales. Check your own parish clerk for its add-ons.

What does Orleans Parish require when a deed is filed?

The Orleans clerk's Land Records Division rejects or surcharges documents with bad margins, and it does not take personal checks. These practical rules come from its published fee sheet and FAQ.

  • The first page needs a two inch top margin, and every page needs one inch at the bottom and both sides, or a $20 surcharge applies.
  • The first page must carry a caption naming the type of act, and the type cannot be smaller than eight point.
  • By mail, send a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court.
  • eRecording is offered through CSC, ePN and Simplifile.
  • A cover sheet marks the document for the mortgage records, the conveyance records or both.

A sale recorded there also triggers the city's documentary transaction tax, which is $325 per taxable document and falls on the seller. It is paid at recording or billed, and a bill unpaid after 30 days adds interest and a $500 penalty.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Louisiana houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When does a transfer of rights work for a seller, and when does it not?

It can fit a transfer between family members, a clean up of a boundary or interest, or a case where the seller honestly cannot vouch for the title. It fits poorly when the buyer is paying full price and needs title insurance.

  • Heirs who have not finished a succession may only hold uncertain rights.
  • A divorce settlement can move one spouse's interest to the other.
  • A buyer who needs the seller to stand behind the title should ask for a full sale with the implied warranty left in place.

An outstanding mortgage, tax lien or judgment is not erased by moving title. A recorded mortgage stays on the record until a cancellation is filed, and Orleans Parish charges $50 to record the cancellation of a single mortgage.

If you want to sell a house with unclear title, an inherited share or a lien, we can read the record with you and explain what a closing would need.

More questions about Louisiana Quitclaim Deed

Is a quitclaim deed valid in Louisiana?

Louisiana has no deed by that name, but article 2502 of the Civil Code lets you transfer the rights you hold without warranting them. The paper in the record is usually an act of sale, donation or transfer of rights. It must still meet the form rules for immovable property.

Does a Louisiana deed need a notary?

A transfer of immovable property can be an authentic act or an act under private signature. An authentic act is signed before a notary or other authorized officer and two witnesses. Most closings use a notary for that reason.

Where do I record a deed in Louisiana?

File it with the clerk of court in the parish where the property is located. The instrument affects third persons only from the time it is filed there. In Orleans Parish, that is the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Louisiana?

The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages. Orleans Parish adds a $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee, and other parishes may add their own charges.

Does the seller still warrant title with a no warranty transfer?

No for the rights themselves. Article 2502 says the transferor does not owe a refund if the buyer is evicted. The seller remains liable for his own acts, since article 2503 voids any agreement that excuses a seller from an eviction he caused.

content:
Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Louisiana House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the official sources say

  • A small succession is a Louisiana-domiciled decedent with property of gross value $200,000 or less at date of death. (La. C.C.P. art. 3421; source)
  • Ancillary small succession: non-Louisiana domiciliary with Louisiana property of $125,000 or less. (La. C.C.P. art. 3421; source)
  • A succession where death occurred at least 20 years before execution of a small succession affidavit qualifies regardless of value. (La. C.C.P. art. 3421; source)
Selling in Louisiana?
We buy Louisiana houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

What is probate called in Louisiana, and where does it happen?

Louisiana calls the process a succession, and the goal is a judgment of possession or an affidavit that shows who now owns the estate. Venue follows the decedent's domicile at death, so the petition goes to the district court for that parish. In Orleans Parish the Civil District Court handles it, according to the Loyola pro bono desk manual.

If the decedent lived outside Louisiana, the succession can be opened in any parish where the person owned immovable property. A seller dealing with an inherited house should first confirm which parish court, or which clerk of court, holds the file.

What is a small succession and what is the dollar limit now?

A small succession is one where the gross value of the estate is $200,000 or less at the date of death, if the decedent was domiciled in Louisiana. That limit is stated in Code of Civil Procedure art. 3421, which also sets a second tier for ancillary successions.

Type of small successionLimit in art. 3421
Decedent domiciled in LouisianaGross value of $200,000 or less at date of death
Decedent domiciled elsewhere, Louisiana property only (ancillary)Gross value of $125,000 or less at date of death
Death at least 20 years before the affidavit is signedNo dollar limit

Older guides, including some law school and title materials, still describe $125,000 as the general cap. The legislature's current article text reads $200,000 for domiciled decedents, so check the date on anything you read.

Who can use the affidavit instead of going to court?

Article 3431 says it is not necessary to open a small succession judicially in three situations. All of them are narrower than they sound, so read the list closely.

  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died without a will.
  • A Louisiana domiciliary who died with a will but left no immovable property in the state, and only if the surviving spouse and every person who would inherit with or without the will agree to waive probate.
  • A non-domiciliary who died without a will, or whose will was probated by court order in another state.

A decedent with a will who owned a house in Louisiana does not fit the second item, because the house is immovable property. That estate needs a judicial route. Paragraph B of the same article also lets a governor-appointed public administrator use the affidavit for small estates with no heir present, after a single advertisement in the official parish journal and no notice of opposition.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Louisiana house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What goes in the small succession affidavit?

Article 3432 covers the intestate affidavit, and it must be sworn by at least two people. When there is a surviving spouse, the spouse signs along with one or more heirs. With no spouse, at least two heirs sign, or one heir and a second person with actual knowledge of the facts if there is only one heir.

  • The date of death, domicile, marital status and last residence of the decedent.
  • Each heir's name, last known address and relationship, and why any non-signing heir did not sign: unlocatable after reasonable diligence, or given 30 days' notice by mail without objecting.
  • A description of the property, labeled community or separate, with enough detail for an immovable to be transferred.
  • The value of each item and the total at death, plus each heir's interest and any usufruct of the surviving spouse.
  • A statement that each signing heir accepts the succession, sworn under penalty of perjury.

Article 3433, added by Acts 2024, No. 90, covers a non-domiciliary who died with a will. It also requires a copy of the will and a certified copy of the other state's probate order, and a legatee's acceptance.

How does the affidavit move title to a house?

The affidavit, or a certified copy, has to be recorded in the conveyance records of the parish where the immovable is located. Article 3434 says a recorded affidavit is admissible and is prima facie evidence of the facts it states, including the heirs' relationship to the decedent and their rights in the property.

The same article lets banks and others holding money or property rely on a multiple original or certified copy as authority to pay or deliver to the named successors, and it discharges them when they do.

There is a catch for anyone left out of the affidavit. A person who claims to be a successor but is not named has two years from the recording date to assert an interest against a third party who acquired the property for value, or that party's successors. Civil Code art. 3338 and R.S. 9:2721 explain why recording in the correct parish matters: an unrecorded instrument has no effect on third persons, and the recorded conveyance must name who pays property tax and give a mailing address for tax notices.

When is a court-run succession needed, and how does it work?

You need a judicial succession when the facts fall outside the affidavit rules, such as a will that has to be probated, a house in a testate estate, or an estate above the dollar limit. The aim is a judgment of possession that recognizes the heirs or legatees and places them in possession.

For an intestate estate that is relatively free from debt, Code of Civil Procedure arts. 3001 through 3008 allow an ex parte petition for possession by all competent heirs who accept the succession. The desk manual says the petition usually comes with an Affidavit of Death, Domicile and Heirship under arts. 2821 and 2822, signed by two people with knowledge. Civil Code art. 962 presumes that a successor accepts unless there is a written renunciation, which is why filings usually include every successor.

For a testate estate, art. 3031 lets a court put legatees in possession on an ex parte petition from all general and universal legatees, provided the will has been probated, each legatee is competent or represented and accepts, and no creditor has demanded administration. The desk manual adds that a will must be probated within five years of the judicial opening of the succession, under art. 2893, and that a succession representative named in the will has to join the petition for possession.

Can a succession representative sell the house?

Yes, by private sale if the court approves it. Under Code of Civil Procedure art. 3281, the representative files a petition describing the property, the price and conditions, and the reasons for selling privately, and attaches any sale agreement already signed.

The representative may sign the agreement first, but it is subject to the suspensive condition that the court approve the sale. The petition is due within 30 days after the agreement is signed.

This timeline matters for heirs who are in a hurry. A buyer can sign a contract while the court paperwork runs, and the closing then waits on the approval.

What does a Louisiana heir face when selling an inherited house?

The common problems are proving who owns the house and paying carrying costs while the paperwork runs.

  • Surviving spouse protections: homestead rights under R.S. 20:1 reach the surviving spouse and minor children of a deceased owner, and the constitutional homestead exemption can continue for a surviving spouse who occupies the home.
  • Property taxes: the tax is a charge on the land, so unpaid balances travel with the house. Redemption after a tax sale costs the taxes, a 5 percent penalty and 1 percent simple interest per month, per the desk manual's chapter on real estate taxes.
  • Storm and flood damage: Louisiana's gulf location and hurricane history, noted in the state overview, can add repair and insurance questions.

A cash buyer will still need the heirs' ownership documents to close. Sorting out the affidavit or judgment first can shorten the process, and a cash buyer who purchases as-is can take over the repair worries that stall many inherited sales.

More questions about Louisiana Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Do I have to go through court to inherit a house in Louisiana?

Not always. If the decedent lived in Louisiana, died without a will, and the estate is $200,000 or less, a small succession affidavit under arts. 3431 and 3432 can work. A will plus a house usually means a judicial succession.

How much is a small succession in Louisiana?

$200,000 or less in gross value for a Louisiana domiciliary, and $125,000 or less for an ancillary succession of someone domiciled elsewhere. A death at least 20 years before the affidavit has no dollar limit under art. 3421.

Who signs a small succession affidavit?

At least two people. If there is a surviving spouse, the spouse signs plus at least one heir. With no spouse, two heirs sign, or one heir and another person with actual knowledge of the facts.

Where is the affidavit recorded?

In the conveyance records of the parish where the house is located, under art. 3434. Banks and other holders of the decedent's money may also rely on a certified copy to pay the named heirs.

Can I sell the house before the succession is finished?

A succession representative can sign a private sale agreement before court approval, but the contract is subject to a suspensive condition that the court approve it. The petition must be filed within 30 days of signing.
